A Response Difference with a Selected Step

Source: R/y_derivatives.R
fd_stable_quotient.Rd

Evaluates a central difference in the response at both steps of fd_steps_y() and keeps, observation by observation, the one that agrees better with itself at half its step. It is the reference check_distrib() compares a family's response derivatives and its distribution function against.

Usage

fd_stable_quotient(quotient, y, bounds, h_rel)

Arguments

quotient

A function of a vector of steps as long as y, returning the difference quotient at those steps. It should divide by the steps at which its evaluation points actually lie, as fd_first_taken() does.

y

The points, a numeric vector.

bounds

The support, a numeric vector of length two.

h_rel

The relative step, a single positive number.

Value

A numeric vector as long as y.

Details

For each of the two steps the quotient \(q(h)\) is also taken at \(h/2\), and its self-consistency is \(|q(h/2) - q(h)|/|q(h)|\): infinite where \(q(h/2)\) is not finite, and undefined where \(q(h)\) is exactly zero. The step scaled on the distance to the bound is kept only where both readings are defined and its own is strictly the smaller; everywhere else, ties included, the clamped step is kept. The value returned is the quotient at the full step.

Neither step is accurate for every family, which is why both are read. Where the log-density is singular at a bound, the error of the clamped step stops falling once the clamp binds; where it is smooth at the bound, the scaled step is the less accurate one at the smallest distances. Where both readings are defined, the clamped step is kept unless the scaled one agrees strictly better with itself at half the step.

In a few cases the scaled step is kept although the clamped step would have been accurate. The scaled numerator is then a whole number of units in the last place of the log-density, which scales exactly with the step, so the quotient agrees with itself at half the step to the last bit and the test reads it as stable.

It costs four quotients where one would do, except where the two steps coincide at every observation, which is every call on a family with no finite bound: there the clamped quotient is returned at once.

Near a bound that is not zero

Near zero the spacing of doubles is relative, so a step scaled on the distance can be as small as the distance requires. Near any other bound the spacing is absolute, one unit of the last place at the bound, and within about \(10^{-10}\) of it two things go wrong. A step that is not a whole number of units is not the step at which the evaluation points lie, so a quotient that divides by the nominal step is out by their rounding; and the scaled step falls below one unit and rounds to zero. The selection rule cannot tell these cases apart, because both candidates come from the same arithmetic. Every candidate step is therefore at least \(2\lvert y\rvert\varepsilon\), which leaves its half step at least one unit long, and the quotient that a caller passes divides by the steps actually taken, as fd_first_taken() and fd_second_taken() do. Neither repair reaches a point within a few units of such a bound, where the relative error of the reference decreases as about \(5.4/d^2\) in the distance \(d\) counted in units; check_distrib() leaves those draws out.

See also

fd_steps_y() for the two steps, check_distrib() for where it is used, fd_first_taken() and fd_second_taken() for quotients on the steps taken.
